clue.text: Is it good to kiss and tell?

definitions.text: Is it good to kiss and tell?

parts.words: Is it good to kiss and tell?
parts.note: kissing a famous stone at an Irish castle is said to grant the gift of the gab, making the kisser good at telling tales

explanation.surface: A question about whether it's wise to reveal one's romantic encounters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kiss and tell' looks like gossip about a lover; the cryptic reading is that kissing this stone makes you good at telling, i.e. eloquent. It is at Blarney Castle near Cork in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says kissing this Irish castle stone bestows eloquence, so it is literally a thing good to kiss in order to talk well.

clue.text: Award without end pitch

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the award goes round the other word

parts.note: a grant is a sum awarded
to die is to come to an end

explanation.surface: A prize given for a pitch that never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking, so the award wraps round the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitch is the steepness of a slope, the same as its incline or slant.

clue.text: Municipal rise and fall

indicators.note: in a down entry the word reads the same going up as coming down, so it can rise and fall unchanged

parts.note: the defining word also supplies the letters, which read the same both ways

explanation.surface: The rise and fall of a town council.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light the answer is a palindrome: it reads identically upwards (rise) and downwards (fall).
explanation.definitionFit: Civic and municipal both describe matters belonging to a town or city and its administration.

clue.text: Bikes initially have come home without a saddle

indicators.note: initially picks out just the opening letter of the word Bikes

parts.note: people who have come home are back

explanation.surface: Cyclists return having ridden without saddles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a saddle' seems to describe the bikes, but it is the definition, describing a way of riding a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding bareback means riding a horse with no saddle on its back.

clue.text: Start to withstand what might go pop?

indicators.note: start to picks only the first letter of the following word

parts.note: an easel is a stand for a painting

explanation.surface: Something about holding firm against a balloon that may burst.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter splits 'withstand' into 'with' and 'stand'. The definition alludes to the nursery rhyme 'Pop goes the weasel'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme line 'Pop goes the weasel', the mustelid is the thing that goes pop.

clue.text: Safe at last, wrapped in cloth, cut off from supernatural stuff

indicators.note: wrapped in says the final letter sits inside the jumbled words
off means not right, so the letters of the two words are jumbled
at last takes only the final letter of the word Safe

explanation.surface: A safe, swathed in fabric, isolated from anything paranormal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' scrambles the two fodder words to THOCCULT, and 'wrapped in' places the E after the first two letters. 'cut off' reads as one phrase but is split between fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: The occult covers magic, spirits and other mystical matters beyond the natural world.

clue.text: Coins wasted securing a better establishment

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the jumbled letters enclose the a
wasted means wrecked, so the letters of Coins are scattered

explanation.surface: Money squandered in getting a superior business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasted' turns COINS into CSINO, and 'securing' puts A inside. 'better' reads as superior, but here it is someone who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambling house is a place of business for people who bet, a bettor's establishment.

clue.text: Underwear storage in artists' bosoms

definitions.meaning: furniture with sliding compartments where knickers (British 'drawers') are kept
artists are those who draw, and bosoms are their breasts or torsos

explanation.surface: Where undies are kept, found in painters' breasts.
explanation.walkthrough: Old British slang calls underpants 'drawers'; an artist is also a 'drawer', and bosoms are 'chests'.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of bedroom furniture with sliding compartments holds clothes; read literally the phrase also means the torsos of people who draw.

clue.text: Tradition to include prom finale in retreat

indicators.note: to include means to take inside, so the heritage word surrounds the letter

parts.note: heritage is the tradition handed down

indicators.note: finale takes the closing letter of the word prom

explanation.surface: A customary practice of ending the Proms is then to withdraw.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are the BBC's summer series of classical concerts in London, ending with the famous Last Night.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit's dwelling is a secluded place of withdrawal, a retreat from the world.

clue.text: Some heartache at home in Hampstead?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A bit of domestic sorrow for someone living in a smart London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampstead is a district in north London famous for its large open park, so the definition is an example of where one is found, signalled by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampstead's famous open common is the archetypal one of these scrubby open spaces, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: What may help sleep is blend regularly used by conservatives

indicators.note: regularly used means only every other letter of blend is taken

parts.note: by as in multiplication, six by four meaning six times four
Tories are members of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A sleep aid made of a mixture that right-wingers take routinely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' gives TIMES as in multiplication; 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tales read aloud to a child at night help the child drift off to sleep.

clue.text: See 11
Ultimately, trivia help me climax? Yes

definitions.text: Ultimately, trivia help me climax? Yes

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the final letter of each following word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether quiz facts will bring them to a peak, and gets an affirmative.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letters of 'trivia', 'help', 'me' and 'climax' spell the answer, while the whole clue also points at a climax; 'Yes' confirms it.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point or culmination of something is its peak or climax.

clue.text: Special 'lorry class' motor race

indicators.note: special suggests a modified version, so the letters of the quoted phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dedicated category of race for heavy goods vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: A lorry is the British word for a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a motorsport event in which cars race on a circuit mixing tarmac and loose surfaces.

clue.text: Little sister hugs so many when playing game

indicators.note: hugs means wraps round, so the short sister word surrounds the jumble

parts.note: sis is the shortened form of sister

indicators.note: when playing suggests the words are moving about, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A small girl cuddles lots of people during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when playing' rearranges the two words to MONSAY, which 'hugs' places inside the short form of sister.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a children's party game in which players obey only instructions prefixed by a fixed phrase.

clue.text: Split hairs? Use a fine-toothed comb

definitions.meaning: literally to pick lice eggs out of hair with a special comb

explanation.surface: Questions and advice about grooming tangled hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: removing head-lice eggs from hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Quibbling over trivia and literally removing louse eggs from hair are both described by this verb.

clue.text: Rich fellow being stupid and loud

indicators.note: being stupid suggests the word is muddled, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: f (forte) is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: A wealthy man who is dim and noisy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being affluent or prosperous means having plenty of money.

clue.text: Get less convincing victory protecting the planet

indicators.note: protecting means covering, so the victory word goes round the planet

parts.note: a win is a victory
our planet is Earth

explanation.surface: A triumph that saves the world becomes less persuasive.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse that wears thin loses credibility through overuse, becoming less persuasive.

clue.text: Elaborate clues to 'a kiss'

indicators.note: elaborate as a verb means to work up or develop, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An instruction to expand the hints that lead to a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elaborate' looks like an adjective or a request for more detail; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a formal, almost scientific verb meaning to kiss.

clue.text: I'm surprised solver's keeping mum

parts.note: the solver is addressed as you, and solver's is read as you are
to keep mum is to stay silent, not to say anything

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished that the puzzler stays silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solver's' stands for 'solver is', so 'you are keeping mum' becomes the phrase; crosswords call the solver 'you'.
explanation.definitionFit: This exclamation expresses mock or genuine astonishment, like saying 'Really?'

clue.text: Uniform: spelled out, it's square

parts.note: Uniform is the NATO radio code word for the letter U

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the spelled-out punctuation mark's letters are jumbled

parts.note: the punctuation mark printed after Uniform, written as a word, is a colon

explanation.surface: Someone spelling out the word uniform declares it fuddy-duddy.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon after 'Uniform' looks like mere punctuation, but it is fodder: written out it is COLON, which 'out' scrambles to NCOOL. 'it's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Square is dated slang for someone conventional and unfashionable, the opposite of hip.

clue.text: Producing a pleasant sensation, half disgustingly

indicators.note: half takes the second six of the twelve letters of disgustingly

explanation.surface: Something feels pleasant but is also somewhat revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half of DISGUSTINGLY gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A prickling, thrilling feeling like goosebumps is a pleasant physical sensation.

clue.text: Scholar missing short holiday as a result of injury

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so those letters are taken out of Scholar

parts.note: hol is a short form of holiday

explanation.surface: An academic who misses a brief break because of being hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark left on the skin after a wound has healed is a lasting result of injury.

clue.text: Lust after firm check

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
to vet is to check thoroughly

explanation.surface: A company examines someone's lustful desires.
explanation.definitionFit: To crave or desire something belonging to another is to lust after it.

clue.text: Feeds well and puts to bed

definitions.meaning: eats heartily, informally diving into a meal
settles a child in bed with the covers secured

explanation.surface: A parent who feeds the child heartily and then sends them to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both eating heartily and securing bedclothes around someone settled for the night.

clue.text: Not fast enough for capital in drag

indicators.note: in says the capital city sits inside the drag word

parts.note: to tow is to drag behind
Oslo is the capital of Norway

explanation.surface: A capital city where drag queens are a bit slow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drag' suggests cross-dressing; here it is pulling.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking enough speed means being sluggish, not quick enough.

clue.text: Sex in the City fine with love …

indicators.note: in says the letters for love and fine go inside the city's abbreviation

parts.note: NY is New York, the city
love is zero in tennis, the shape of the letter O
OK means fine

explanation.surface: Nods to the TV show 'Sex and the City', a fine romantic comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes the New York TV series 'Sex and the City'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is informal British slang for sexual intercourse.

clue.text: … and another lie about another secret

indicators.note: about means all around, so the letters of lie and secret are mixed up

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, another falsehood about yet another secret.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links it to 26: after New York, 'another' city. 'another' before 'secret' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Following the city in the previous clue, 'another' means another city, and this is an English city in the Midlands.
